extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of logic/epistemology; those studying induction, syllogism, and reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and evaluate the logical role and limits of the syllogism, the relation between particular observations and general propositions, and the proper function of generalization and interpretation in reasoning. Emphasizes when syllogisms are merely records and when induction or hermeneutics is the real operative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of petitio principii in every syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: In every syllogism, considered as an argument to prove the conclusion, there is a petitio principii — the general premise already presupposes what is asserted in the particular conclusion (e.g., 'All men are mortal' presupposes 'Socrates is mortal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the objection raised by adversaries of the syllogistic theory: a general principle cannot be taken for true without independent evidence that the particulars it covers actually satisfy it. The text presents the objection and shows it is 'irrefragable' unless one distinguishes stages of reasoning (see registration vs inference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inference (origin) from registering/notation (recording)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the act of inferring with the act of recording or registering that inference (the mistake of referring to one's notes as the origin of knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: knowing 'The Duke of Wellington is mortal' is not really 'inferred from' the generalization in one’s notes; the inference (inductive warrant) arises from observed particulars and not from the memorandum. Treat notes as reminders, not as the primary source. Anti-pattern: attributing explanatory power to a written generality rather than to the underlying observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: All genuine inference originates from particulars (induction first)
rubrics_metrics.description: All inference is fundamentally from particulars to particulars; general propositions are aggregates or compendia of particular inferences rather than their origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization compresses past observations plus the inferences drawn from them. The real logical antecedents are the particular facts from which general propositions were collected by induction. Thus, when evaluating reasoning, check the supporting particulars and whether induction from them is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism's proper function is interpretation/consistency, not origination
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogism functions to interpret a memorandum or authoritative generality and to ensure consistency between conclusions drawn in particular cases and prior general directions; it is a mode of interpretation (hermeneutics) rather than the primary process of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When premises derive from testimony or law, reasoning is inquiry into the witness’s or legislator’s intention by examining marks/signs. The rules of the syllogism serve to maintain consistency between conclusions and previously laid down general propositions. Analogy: judge interpreting law; memorandum interpreted to avoid drawing inferences not conformable to former intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of the syllogism are precautions to insure correct interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogistic rules are a set of precautions designed to ensure we correctly read and apply the record (general proposition) derived from past observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules guard against misapplication of generalities and preserve logical consistency. In practice, they operate as checks that what is read off a general formula legitimately follows from the underlying particulars; view them as safeguards rather than the source of evidentiary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions are useful shorthand and testing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions compress many observed instances and the inferences drawn from them into a single, concise expression that records both what has been observed and what is inferred from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulating the broadest appropriate general theorem is important: it presents a larger object to imagination (leading to more careful weighing of evidence) and helps detect insufficiency of premises by including potential counterinstances. Example: considering whether evidence that supports belief about Commodus would justify a general 'all emperors are just' would reveal counterexamples like Nero, exposing insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalization to detect insufficient evidence via reductio
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning a particular inference into a general proposition allows one to test the sufficiency of evidence by checking for known counter-cases; if the generalization would imply false instances, the evidence is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: if a proposed particular conclusion would warrant asserting a general class, inspect all cases in that class for contradictions; known counterexamples reveal inadequate grounds. This is an explicit advantage of arguing via induction + syllogistic application rather than directly from particulars to particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is legitimate and common to reason directly from particular to particular
rubrics_metrics.description: One may often reason directly from observed particulars to other particulars without passing through explicit general propositions (e.g., a child or an animal inferring from one burned instance to avoid fire in another case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: burned child/dog, craftsmen with tacit knowledge, experienced generals making quick judgments. Anti-pattern: insisting on explicit intermediate general statements when practical immediate inferences from particulars suffice; yet note the explanatory and communicative benefits of generalizing where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms/definitions are convenient assumptions, not metaphysical origins of demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrations (e.g., geometry) the particular instance (diagram) often suffices for assent to a conclusion; axioms and definitions act as shorthand notices of assumptions, not mystical sources of new truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: demonstrating a property for circle ABC appeals to the particular instance; axioms/definitions announce which assumptions one intends to make in all analogous cases. Practical implication: when reviewing proofs or demonstrations, check the particular assumptions in the concrete case as well as the claimed general axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: When premises are authoritative (testimony/command), reasoning is hermeneutic
rubrics_metrics.description: If the available generalities come from authority (witness testimony, scripture, law), the inferential task reduces to determining whether the authoritative statement was meant to include the present case by examining signs/marks — an interpretive task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the authority intended the present case to be covered by their general statement. This shifts focus from 'does the general imply the particular?' to 'did the authority intend the general to apply here?'; treat as a question of interpretation with its own rules.
